title: the lint gate sizes its parallel run by CPUs and never by memory, so a host with many CPUs and too little memory has checks killed, each read as a breach
body:
## Problem

`gate_lint` (bin/.devbin/cmd/.lib/shell-gate:126-128) runs as many checks at once as `nproc` says, capped at 8, and asks nothing about memory. `shellcheck -x` is heavy on devbin's larger files: on macOS, shellcheck 0.11.0 peaks at 2.17 GB resident on bin/devbin, and at 1.0 to 1.3 GB on four of lib/cmd's handlers, so the eight largest at once need about 8.69 GB and the four largest about 5.71 GB. Where that much is not free, the kernel kills checks. A killed check's worker records 137 with "Killed" as the file's output, and the gate counts the file as a breach. That fails closed, so it is never a false green; it is a red with no defect behind it, and it is likeliest on the hosts with the most CPUs.

## Measured

- vc, on this Mac: `/usr/bin/time -l shellcheck -x bin/devbin`, maximum resident set size 2,167,865,344 bytes, 22.8 s.
- dc, for 0180 (its Resolution's last paragraph): the 1.0 to 1.3 GB on four handlers and the two sums above. In an ubuntu:24.04 container in a 4 GiB VM with eight CPUs, unpinned, the kernel killed shellcheck 14 times in one gate (the VM's kernel log, 0.52 to 1.2 GB resident at each kill), with d7f2ed13's gate and with 0180's alike. Pinned to two CPUs, the same gate over the tree is clean.
- CI's Ubuntu runner ran the gate over the tree, in contract.bats's lint arm, on run 37578519788 without a kill.

## Fix

A file whose check was killed by a signal (status above 128), or that was left with no verdict, is checked again alone after the parallel run, before it counts. A kill under memory pressure then passes or fails on its own terms, and a check killed when run alone is still a breach. The second run is said, eg "lint: lib/x was killed (137) in the parallel run; checked again alone: ok". A check that failed on its own terms (status 1) is never run again, so a real breach costs nothing more. Sizing the run by free memory is the alternative, and it needs a reading of free memory on each platform, which a second run does not.

## Done when

1. A fake shellcheck killed by a signal on its first run of a file and passing on its second leaves that file no breach, with the second run said; the arm is red on main first.
2. A file killed on its second run as well is a breach, and a file whose check exits 1 is a breach and is not run again.
3. 0155's and 0180's lint arms still hold: a worker that dies leaves its file no verdict until the second run, whose result they read.

## Resolution

Landed at 16599f4d on a green full suite (vc's, 2243 of 2243 ok, 0 not ok, .errors empty, seal 20261008-0655).

1. A file whose check exited above 128 in the parallel run, or that the parallel run left with no verdict or never started, is checked by itself once every worker of the parallel run has exited, and that verdict is the one that counts. A line says both: `lint: lib/x exited 137 in the parallel run; checked again alone: ok`, with `exited N` or `no verdict` in place of `ok` when the file fails there too; `had no verdict from the parallel run; checked again alone: ...` for a file whose worker died; `was not checked in the parallel run; checked alone: ...` for one xargs never started, which 0155 declared a breach. A check that failed on its own terms, a status from 1 to 128, is never run again, so a real breach costs nothing more and is printed once. A host short of memory now pays for its kills in time, one check at a time, rather than in breaches with no defect behind them.
2. The line gives the status rather than naming a kill, since a status above 128 is not always a signal: `shellcheck -x bin/devbin` under `ulimit -v` at 300000, 600000 and 1200000 KiB exits 251 with "shellcheck: out of memory", and such a file is checked again too.
3. One function, `lint_checks`, runs the check and 0180's wait at either width: the parallel run over the corpus, and each second run at one job, one file to an xargs, so a worker killed in one file's second run stops no other file's. One function, `lint_verdict`, gives each file's verdict, its second run included, and the read-back loop is one line per file. `lint: no verdict for <f>` is gone, since every such file is now checked alone; the second run's xargs status is said as the parallel run's always was: `lint: the run of <f> alone exited N`.

The arms, in contract.bats, all five carrying 0184 in their titles:

- A check killed in the parallel run, by SIGKILL and in a second file by SIGTERM, while another check runs, is checked again alone and passes: no breach, both lines, the second runs' output printed and the killed checks' never, each killed file checked twice and the other once, and xargs not failing. The fake makes the overlap with the running check and checks it, and each second run looks for any other running check as it starts and as it ends, so a second run inside the parallel run, or two second runs at once, turns it red.
- A check killed in both runs is a breach whose line gives both statuses, 137 then 143, so the second is read from the second run; a check that exits 1 is a breach, checked once, its finding printed once.
- A file xargs never started, once a worker dies at two jobs, is checked alone and passes, beside xargs's own words for the death.
- 0155's arm reads the second run: its lever fires on every check of lib/dies, so the file still has no verdict, a breach, and the arm asserts the line and the second run's exit. 0180's arm asserts that no file was checked alone: a gate that stopped waiting would check lib/clean alone and pass it.
- One helper builds the probe and the fakes, owns their paths, and checks that the gate made its scratch under TMPDIR and removed it; one names the files checked alone, keyed on the line's fixed end; one counts the fake's calls. The lever helper requires shellcheck and checks that the lever fired before it trusts its overlap check.

Evidence, in ~/Devel/scratch/devbin-dc/0184/runs/, at aed7af10, the patch's commit in the scratch clone (v21-mac-{bsd,gnu}-20261007-130730.log, ubuntu-v21-20261007-131816.log, targeted-v21-{bsd,gnu}-20261007-131816.log):

- Red on main first, the issue's Done when 1: main's gate, b6a39287's, where 0180 landed, and unchanged on main since, turns 0155's arm and the three new arms red, on macOS under BSD tools and with GNU tools first on PATH, and 3 of 3 in an ubuntu:24.04 container; 0180's arm passes there, since main waits. 0.1.9's gate, d7f2ed13's, turns all five red, 0180's included, since it predates 0180.
- Green: the five arms, 3 of 3 on macOS under BSD tools and with GNU tools first on PATH, and 3 of 3 in the container.
- Mutants, 21, each applied once, parsed, and red at its aimed arm on macOS under both tool sets and in the container: 26 of 26 sections as aimed under each tool set on macOS and 28 of 28 in the container, where main ran three times. 0184's fifteen: no second run; a check that exited 1 run again; the second run's status never read; the second run not said; the check run again inside the worker, during the parallel run; the second runs in one batch at the parallel run's width; the line's second status the first run's; only SIGKILL's status checked again; a second run with no verdict not said as one; a file whose worker died never checked again; a file never started said as one with no verdict; a file never started never checked; a killed check's first output printed; a file checked alone never having its output printed; and the gate's scratch made outside TMPDIR. 0180's five, re-expressed on 0184's gate: a subshell between the worker and shellcheck, pipefail off in gate_lint, a worker program that redirects its own stdout, the arms' fake nproc at 1, and that with a gate that prints no file's output. And the lever helper's checks pointed at another directory, where its overlap check would pass by reading nothing.
- The case, in the container, a 4 GiB VM with eight CPUs, the gate unpinned: main's gate over the tree exits 1 in 168 s, 48 files, 6 breaches, each a check killed with 137; 0184's exits 0 in 331 s, 0 breaches, its six killed files checked again alone and each ok: bin/devbin, lib/cmd/check, lib/cmd/docs, lib/cmd/doctor, lib/cmd/dormancy and lib/cmd/fullcycle. The VM's kernel log records the kills as out-of-memory kills of shellcheck. v2's container run killed the same six files, and took 132 s on main and 262 s with the fix. Under `ulimit -v` at 300000, 600000 and 1200000 KiB, `shellcheck -x bin/devbin` exits 251 with "shellcheck: out of memory", point 2's status.
- contract.bats whole, in the container pinned to two CPUs: 41 of 41, none skipped, so 0155's and 0180's arms hold beside the new ones, the issue's Done when 3.
- The targeted run (contract, helpers, neutral, documentation, readonlygit, harness and help): 272 of 272 under BSD tools and 272 of 272 with GNU tools first on PATH, the tree clean at aed7af10 before and after; the only skips are require_command's own two. Its lint arm reads the tree as 48 files and 0 breaches under both.
- critic-shell reviewed the first build (no critical, one warning, seven recommendations and four style points) and the second (no critical, two warnings, two recommendations and three style points). This patch folds the second set in as the critic gave it, and was not reviewed a third time. From the first, two points were not taken: a helper for reading a status file, and letting the check hold the pipe, which is the first declared limit below.

Declared limits:

- A check whose worker was killed can still be running when its file's second run starts, so that run is not alone. The kernel short of memory kills the largest process, the check, not its worker, so the out-of-memory case leaves no such orphan. Letting the check hold the pipe too would close it, and was not taken: it extends 0180's wait to such orphans, and a hung check whose worker was killed would then hold the gate.
- The second runs are one at a time, each taking a check's whole time alone. In the container, 0184's gate took 331 s over the tree with six checked again, where main's took 168 s and failed; v2's run of the same comparison took 262 s and 132 s.
- A check that never returns holds the gate, in the second run as in the parallel run.
- The gate still sizes its parallel run by CPUs; the issue's alternative, sizing it by free memory, was not taken.
